title: Blockchain & Decentralized Finance (DeFi)
tagline: Automated market makers, liquidity, lending, oracles, stablecoins and the risks, explained with working teaching contracts
summary: A rigorous, honest introduction to decentralised finance for developers: the building blocks and composability, stablecoin designs and their failures, the constant-product automated market maker with a complete teaching contract, liquidity provision and impermanent loss with real numbers, lending markets with health factors, interest curves and liquidations, flash loans, oracles and time-weighted prices, the sources of yield, the patterns behind major exploits and a due-diligence method. All Solidity listings were compiled with solc against OpenZeppelin 5. The course is educational only: it is not financial, investment or legal advice, and the contracts are not audited and must not hold real funds.

modules.title: DeFi foundations
modules.summary: What decentralised finance is, its building blocks, composability, stablecoins and honest comparisons with traditional finance.
modules.outcome: You can describe the main DeFi building blocks, explain composability and judge a stablecoin's reserves.
modules.intro: Decentralised finance rebuilds financial functions such as trading, lending and saving as smart contracts that anyone can use. It has produced genuine innovation and spectacular losses. This course explains how the pieces work so you can build and judge them with open eyes. It is education only and not financial advice.

topics.title: Financial functions as code
topics.html:
Traditional finance relies on institutions: exchanges, banks and clearing houses that hold your assets and enforce rules. DeFi moves some of those functions into smart contracts. You keep your assets in your own wallet until you choose to interact, and the rules are public code rather than private agreements. This removes some kinds of trust and adds others: you must now trust the code, its authors and its dependencies.

Traditional finance and DeFi, compared honestly
FeatureTraditional financeDeFi
Who holds your assetsAn institutionYou, until you deposit into a contract
Opening hoursBusiness hoursAll day, every day
AccessAccounts, identity checks, geographyAnyone with a wallet (subject to local law)
TransparencyLimitedCode and transactions are public
ProtectionsDeposit insurance, courts, regulatorsMostly none: mistakes and exploits are usually final
Speed of settlementDaysSeconds to minutes
Typical failureFraud, mismanagement, runsBugs, oracle attacks, key theft, rug pulls

Check what you just learned

1. What new trust does DeFi require?
  • No trust at all
  • Trust in a central bank
  • Trust in the code, its authors and its dependencies (correct)
  • Trust in the weather

Trust moves; it does not vanish.

Watch out

This course is educational and not financial advice. DeFi can lose all your money, and most people should not use it with money they cannot afford to lose.

Check what you just learned

1. In DeFi, deposit insurance is usually:
  • Free
  • Automatic
  • Guaranteed by law
  • Absent (correct)

Few protections exist.
keyPoints: DeFi turns financial functions into public smart contracts.
It removes some trust and adds trust in code.

topics.title: Building blocks and composability
topics.html:
The main blocks
BlockJobExample behaviour
Decentralised exchange (DEX)Swap tokensPools priced by a formula
Lending marketLend and borrow against collateralInterest follows supply and demand
StablecoinA steady unit of accountBacked by assets or collateral
OracleBring outside data on-chainPrices, interest rates, events
DerivativesTrade exposure to pricesFutures, options
Aggregators and vaultsAutomate strategies across protocolsMove funds to the best return

DeFi pieces are open, so one protocol can use another as a component. A vault may deposit into a lending market, which uses an oracle that reads a DEX, whose pools hold stablecoins. This composability is powerful, because new products appear without permission, and dangerous, because a failure in one piece can travel through every piece built on it.

Check what you just learned

1. What risk does composability create?
  • A failure in one component can spread through everything built on it (correct)
  • Nothing, it is only good
  • Higher gas only
  • Lower transparency

Dependencies chain risks together.

Check what you just learned

1. Composability means protocols can:
  • Merge into one
  • Use one another as components (correct)
  • Hide from users
  • Print money

Open building blocks.
keyPoints: Exchanges, lending, stablecoins, oracles and vaults are the main blocks.
Composability creates opportunity and chains risk.

topics.title: Stablecoins: promises of stability
topics.html:
Kinds of stablecoin
KindHow it aims to hold its valueMain risks
Fiat-backedReserves of cash and short-term government debt back each tokenIssuer honesty, bank and custody risk, freezing, regulation
Crypto-collateralisedOver-collateralised loans in volatile crypto; automatic liquidationsSharp crashes, oracle failures, liquidation congestion
AlgorithmicSupply is adjusted by rules or a companion tokenConfidence spirals; several have collapsed to zero
Commodity-backedTied to a physical asset such as goldCustody, audit and redemption difficulty

Reserve backing

Change the reserves and tokens in circulation to see the backing ratio. A teaching tool, not an assessment of any real coin.

Adjust Cash and bills (millions), Other assets (millions), Tokens in circulation (millions) and see Backing ratio (%), Cash and bills as a share of tokens (%) change.

What to look for in a stablecoin

  1. Who issues it and under what regulation?
  2. What backs it, and how liquid are those assets?
  3. Are there regular, independent attestations or audits?
  4. Can holders redeem directly, and at what cost?
  5. What happens in a crisis: freezes, delays, liquidations?
  6. How has it behaved during past market stress?

Check what you just learned

1. Why are algorithmic stablecoins considered especially risky?
  • They are too transparent
  • They cost too much
  • Their stability can depend on confidence and a companion token, and a loss of confidence can collapse them (correct)
  • They have too many reserves

Several have failed.

Check what you just learned

1. A backing ratio under 100% means:
  • Nothing
  • Fully backed
  • Overbacked
  • Reserves do not cover all tokens (correct)

A shortfall.

Key terms: flip and sort

DeFi
Decentralised finance built from smart contracts
Composability
Protocols usable as parts of one another
Stablecoin
A token designed to hold a steady value
Oracle
A source of outside data for contracts
Reserve
Assets held to back tokens
Peg
The target price a stablecoin aims to hold
keyPoints: Fiat-backed, crypto-collateralised and algorithmic coins carry different risks.
Check reserves, redemption and past stress behaviour.

modules.title: Automated market makers
modules.summary: The constant-product rule, quotes, slippage and fees, with a complete teaching contract.
modules.outcome: You can calculate a swap by hand, explain slippage and read a simple AMM contract.
modules.intro: The automated market maker replaced the order book with a formula. It is simple enough to understand completely, which makes it the ideal first DeFi contract to read and the foundation for much of what follows.

topics.title: The constant-product rule
topics.html:
A pool holds reserves of two tokens, A and B. The rule is that the product reserve A times reserve B stays constant when someone trades (apart from fees, which make it grow). If a trader adds some B to the pool, the pool must give out enough A to keep the product the same. The price of A in terms of B is simply reserve B divided by reserve A, so it moves as the reserves move.

An example with numbers
StepReserve AReserve BProductPrice of A
Start1,0002,000,0002,000,000,0002,000 B
Trader adds 20,000 B (ignoring fees)about 990.12,020,000about 2,000,000,000about 2,040 B
Trader receivesabout 9.9 AAverage price paid about 2,020 B

Constant-product swap

Change the pool size and the amount you spend to see what you receive and the price impact. Fee 0.3%.

Adjust Reserve of A, Reserve of B, B spent and see A received, Price impact (%) change.

Check what you just learned

1. What happens to the price of A when a trader buys A with B?
  • It rises (correct)
  • It falls
  • It stays the same
  • It becomes zero

The pool has less A and more B.

Check what you just learned

1. The price of A in the pool equals:
  • Reserve A divided by reserve B
  • Reserve B divided by reserve A (correct)
  • Reserve A plus reserve B
  • The product

The ratio of reserves.
keyPoints: Reserve A times reserve B stays constant; the price is the reserve ratio.
Bigger trades relative to the pool move the price more.

topics.title: A teaching AMM contract
topics.html:
Key ideas in the code
IdeaWhere and why
getAmountOutApplies the fee and the formula; a pure function everyone can check
MINIMUM_LIQUIDITY burned at the startStops the first provider manipulating the share price
Shares for the smaller sideAn unbalanced deposit gifts the extra to the pool
minOut and minSharesProtect users when the price moves before inclusion
Reserves recorded in storageThe contract does not trust its raw balance
Effects before transfers and nonReentrantDefence against reentrancy
SafeERC20Handles tokens that do not return values
Watch out

This is a teaching contract. It does not handle fee-on-transfer or rebasing tokens, has no protocol fee and has not been audited. Never deploy it with real funds.

Check what you just learned

1. Why take shares from the smaller side of a deposit?
  • It saves gas
  • Because tokens are equal
  • So a provider cannot claim more of the pool than they put in (correct)
  • It is a Solidity rule

Protect existing providers.

Check what you just learned

1. A minimum output on a swap protects against:
  • Roles
  • Gas
  • Events
  • The price moving before inclusion (correct)

Slippage and front-running.
keyPoints: The contract tracks reserves, mints shares and enforces the formula.
Slippage limits protect users from price moves.

topics.title: The maths in code, and what traders face
topics.html:
What traders must watch
IssueExplanationDefence
SlippageLarge trades relative to the pool get a worse average priceCheck the quoted impact; split trades; use deeper pools
Front-runningA bot sees your pending trade and trades first to profit from the price moveSet a tight minimum output; use private submission services
Sandwich attackA bot trades before and after you, taking value from your slippage allowanceKeep slippage tolerance small
Fake tokensScam tokens with the same nameUse verified addresses only
ApprovalsUnlimited allowances to a routerApprove only what you need

Check what you just learned

1. Why does a wide slippage tolerance help attackers?
  • A bot can move the price within your tolerance and keep the difference (correct)
  • It does not
  • It raises gas
  • It blocks trades

Your tolerance is their profit margin.

Tip

Always compare the price impact with the fee. A trade with 3% impact in a 0.3% fee pool is really a 3% cost.

Check what you just learned

1. A sandwich attack profits from:
  • Your gas
  • Your allowed slippage (correct)
  • Your name
  • Your wallet brand

Tighten it.

Key terms: flip and sort

AMM
Automated market maker
Constant product
The rule that reserve A times reserve B stays constant
Slippage
The gap between the expected and the received price
Liquidity
Tokens in a pool available for trading
Sandwich attack
Trading before and after a victim's trade
Fee tier
The percentage of each trade kept by the pool
keyPoints: Slippage, front-running and sandwich attacks are real costs for traders.
Keep tolerances tight and approvals small.

modules.title: Liquidity provision and impermanent loss
modules.summary: Why providers earn fees, how impermanent loss arises and how to calculate it honestly.
modules.outcome: You can calculate impermanent loss, compare it with fee income and describe the risks of providing liquidity.
modules.intro: Pools need people to supply tokens. Providers earn fees, but they carry risks that are easy to miss: the pool automatically sells the winning token as its price rises, so a provider can end up with less than they would have by simply holding. This module puts numbers on that.

topics.title: Why providers get paid, and what they give up
topics.html:
Sources of return and risk
ItemDirectionNotes
Trading feesIncomeDepends on trading volume and the share of the pool
Reward tokensIncome, if the token holds valueMay fall in price quickly
Impermanent lossCostArises when relative prices diverge
Smart contract riskCostA bug can lose everything
Token riskCostOne token might collapse or be a scam
Gas costsCostEntering and exiting cost fees

Check what you just learned

1. What do pool shares represent?
  • A loan
  • A vote
  • A fraction of the pool's reserves and future fees (correct)
  • A guarantee of profit

Your slice of the pool.

Watch out

Educational only. Providing liquidity can lose money, and promised yields are not guaranteed.

Check what you just learned

1. Fees are earned in proportion to:
  • Your luck
  • Your wallet age
  • Your gas
  • Your share of the pool (correct)

Fees are shared in proportion to each share.
keyPoints: Providers earn fees and face impermanent loss and contract risk.
Pool shares represent a fraction of the reserves.

topics.title: Impermanent loss, with numbers
topics.html:
The idea in one line
QuantityFormula
Impermanent loss for a 50/50 constant-product pool2 × √r ÷ (1 + r) − 1, where r is the new price divided by the old price
Value of the pool position compared with holdingHeld value × (1 + loss), where the loss is negative
Impermanent loss for a 50/50 pool
Relative price changeLoss versus holding
1.25 timesAbout 0.6%
1.5 timesAbout 2.0%
2 timesAbout 5.7%
3 timesAbout 13.4%
5 timesAbout 25.5%
Falls to a tenth (ratio 0.1)About 42%

Impermanent loss calculator

Change the relative price ratio to see the loss compared with holding. A teaching model for a 50/50 constant-product pool.

Adjust Price ratio (new relative to old), Deposit (rupees) and see Impermanent loss (%), Value if held (rupees), Value in the pool before fees (rupees) change.

Check what you just learned

1. When does impermanent loss disappear?
  • If the relative price returns to its starting value (correct)
  • Never
  • When fees are paid
  • After a week

It is a function of the price ratio.

Check what you just learned

1. A price ratio of 1 gives:
  • Total loss
  • No impermanent loss (correct)
  • Double value
  • A fee

No divergence.
keyPoints: Loss is a function of the price ratio: small for small moves, large for big ones.
It becomes real only when you withdraw after divergence.

topics.title: Fees versus loss, and honest expectations
topics.html:
Whether providing liquidity pays depends on whether fee income exceeds the loss from price divergence plus costs. Stable pairs, where both tokens track the same value, have little divergence and modest fees. Volatile pairs have bigger fees if trading is busy, but larger divergence. There is no universal answer, and past fee income does not predict the future.

Typical pair types
Pair typeDivergenceFee incomeSpecial risk
Two stablecoinsVery smallLowA peg failure
Major token with a stablecoinModerate to largeModerate to highLarge price swings
Two correlated tokensSmallModerateCorrelation can break
A new small token with a stablecoinVery largeVariableScams and collapse

Questions to ask before providing liquidity (for study)

  1. What is the pool's trading volume compared with its size?
  2. How large could price divergence be?
  3. Are the tokens and the contract trustworthy?
  4. What are the entry and exit costs?
  5. Can I explain the risks in my own words?
  6. Can I afford to lose this money?

Check what you just learned

1. Why is the past fee yield a poor guide to the future?
  • It is secret
  • Fees are fixed
  • Volume and prices change, so yields change (correct)
  • It is always lower

Conditions move.

Check what you just learned

1. A pool of two stablecoins has:
  • No fees
  • Huge divergence
  • No risk
  • Little divergence but also lower fees (correct)

A different risk profile.

Key terms: flip and sort

Liquidity provider
Someone who deposits tokens into a pool
Pool share
A token representing a fraction of a pool
Impermanent loss
The shortfall of a pool position versus holding
Volume
The amount traded in a period
Divergence
A change in the relative price of the two tokens
Peg
The intended steady price
keyPoints: Providing liquidity pays only if fees exceed divergence loss and costs.
Past yields do not predict future yields.

modules.title: Lending and borrowing
modules.summary: Collateral, interest curves, health factors and liquidations.
modules.outcome: You can compute borrowing limits and health factors, read an interest-rate curve and explain how liquidations protect lenders.
modules.intro: DeFi lending is almost always over-collateralised: you must lock more value than you borrow, because there is no way to chase a borrower who walks away. This module covers the maths of safety, the curve that sets interest, and the mechanism that keeps lenders whole.

topics.title: Collateral, limits and health
topics.html:
Terms
TermMeaningExample
CollateralAssets locked to secure a loan100,000 rupees of a volatile token
Loan-to-value (LTV)The most you can borrow as a share of collateral75% gives 75,000 rupees
Liquidation thresholdThe ratio at which the position becomes unsafe80%
Health factorCollateral × threshold ÷ debt100,000 × 0.8 ÷ 60,000 = 1.33
Liquidation bonusThe discount a liquidator earns5%
UtilisationBorrowed ÷ deposited80% means 80 of every 100 are lent out

Check what you just learned

1. What does a health factor below 1 mean?
  • The position can be liquidated (correct)
  • The loan is safe
  • Interest is zero
  • The loan is repaid

Collateral no longer covers the debt with a margin.

Check what you just learned

1. LTV caps:
  • Your gas
  • How much you can borrow (correct)
  • Your fees
  • Your votes

A share of collateral value.
keyPoints: Over-collateralisation and health factors protect lenders.
Health factor below 1 means liquidation is allowed.

topics.title: Interest rates that follow utilisation
topics.html:
A lending pool must keep enough unlent funds so depositors can withdraw. Interest rates are therefore set by utilisation. When little is borrowed, rates are low to encourage borrowing. When utilisation gets close to 100%, rates climb steeply so that borrowers repay and new deposits arrive. The kinked curve in the contract does exactly this.

Interest rate curve

Move utilisation to see the borrow rate and the deposit rate. The curve: 2% base, 4% slope below an 80% kink, 75% slope above. Reserve factor 10%. A teaching model.

Adjust Utilisation (%) and see Borrow rate (% a year) change.

What the curve achieves
RegionRate behaviourPurpose
Below the kinkGentle riseCheap borrowing keeps the pool useful
Above the kinkVery steep risePull funds back before withdrawals become impossible
At 100%Very highDepositors cannot withdraw; the market is stressed

Check what you just learned

1. Why does the rate rise steeply above the kink?
  • To raise profits
  • To discourage deposits
  • To pull funds back so depositors can still withdraw (correct)
  • To confuse users

Protect liquidity.

Check what you just learned

1. Utilisation is:
  • Price times supply
  • Deposited minus borrowed
  • Fees divided by gas
  • Borrowed divided by deposited (correct)

The share lent out.
keyPoints: Rates follow utilisation along a kinked curve.
Steep rates near full utilisation protect withdrawals.

topics.title: Liquidations and flash loans
topics.html:
Liquidations rely on market participants noticing and acting quickly. In a sharp crash, prices can fall faster than liquidators can act, networks can congest, and oracles can lag. The result can be bad debt: debt that exceeds collateral and falls on depositors.

Flash loans in context
FactExplanation
Borrow any amount with no collateralRepayment is checked inside the same transaction
If not repaid, the transaction revertsAs if it never happened
Legitimate usesRefinancing, arbitrage, self-liquidation, swapping collateral
Attack usesMoving prices to manipulate oracles, or voting power for governance attacks
DefenceDo not use a single spot price; use time-weighted averages and sanity checks

Check what you just learned

1. How does a flash loan avoid needing collateral?
  • Repayment is verified inside the same transaction, or everything is undone (correct)
  • It uses a bank
  • It trusts the borrower
  • It charges a deposit

Atomicity makes it safe for the lender.

Watch out

Education only. Never use flash loans or liquidation bots with real funds without deep understanding and professional review.

Check what you just learned

1. Bad debt is:
  • Old debt
  • Debt exceeding collateral (correct)
  • A kind of interest
  • A fee

Falls on depositors.

Key terms: flip and sort

Over-collateralised
Locking more value than you borrow
Health factor
A safety measure for a position
Liquidation
Forced repayment through sale of collateral
Utilisation
The share of deposits that is lent out
Bad debt
Debt not covered by collateral
Flash loan
A loan repaid in the same transaction
keyPoints: Liquidators repay debt for collateral plus a bonus; crashes can still cause bad debt.
Flash loans work because of atomicity; they also power attacks.

modules.title: Oracles, stablecoin design and yield
modules.summary: Manipulation-resistant prices, how stablecoins fail and where yield really comes from.
modules.outcome: You can read a TWAP oracle, explain stablecoin failure modes and test a yield claim.
modules.intro: Three questions sit under almost every large DeFi loss: where did the price come from, what actually backed the stable asset, and who was paying the yield? This module teaches you to ask them.

topics.title: Prices contracts can trust
topics.html:
Oracle design choices
ChoiceStrengthWeakness
Spot price from one poolSimple and always availableA flash loan can move it in one transaction
Time-weighted average from a deep poolCostly to manipulate over many blocksLags real moves; useless for thin pools
Decentralised oracle networkMany independent reporters and sourcesCost, latency and the trust placed in the network
Multiple sources comparedResists a single failureMore code and complexity
Circuit breakersStop on strange jumpsCan freeze markets when prices move for real

Checks any price consumer should make

  1. The price is not zero or negative.
  2. The price is fresh: updated within an agreed time.
  3. The change from the last price is plausible.
  4. A second source agrees within a tolerance.
  5. What happens when the oracle fails: pause or fallback, not guess.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is a TWAP harder to manipulate than a spot price?
  • It is secret
  • It uses more gas
  • An attacker would need to hold the distorted price for the whole averaging period, which is costly (correct)
  • It is a different token

Time is expensive for an attacker.

Check what you just learned

1. A stale price is dangerous because:
  • It is free
  • It is slower
  • It is private
  • Liquidations may use wrong values (correct)

Old data, wrong decisions.
keyPoints: Spot prices can be manipulated; averages and multiple sources raise the cost.
Always check freshness, sanity and failure behaviour.

topics.title: How stable assets fail
topics.html:
Failure modes
KindHow it failsWarning signs
AlgorithmicA confidence spiral where the backing token loses value as it is createdStability depends on a rising companion token
Crypto-collateralisedCollateral crashes faster than liquidations can runIlliquid collateral, one oracle, congestion
Fiat-backedReserves are not what is claimed, or a custodian failsVague reserve reporting, concentration in one bank
AnyA smart contract exploit or key compromiseUnaudited code, single admin key

The common thread is that stability is a promise, and promises are only as good as the assets and mechanisms behind them in the worst moment. Study how a coin behaved in the worst week of its history, not its calm months.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a warning sign of an algorithmic stablecoin?
  • Stability that relies on constant growth of a companion token (correct)
  • Fully published reserves
  • Regular audits
  • Redemption in cash

Reflexive designs are fragile.

Check what you just learned

1. A confidence spiral is:
  • A price chart
  • Selling causing more selling (correct)
  • A fee
  • An audit

Self-reinforcing.
keyPoints: Stablecoins fail through spirals, crashes, hidden reserves or exploits.
Study behaviour in stress, not in calm.

topics.title: Where does yield come from?
topics.html:
Sources of yield
SourceSustainable?Notes
Trading feesYes, if there is real volumeVaries with markets
Borrower interestYes, if demand is realFalls when borrowing is low
Staking rewards of a networkYes, funded by network designLocked funds and slashing risk
Reward tokens issued by the protocolOnly as long as the token holds valueOften inflates away
Deposits of new usersNoDepends on endless growth: a Ponzi structure
Hidden riskLooks like yield until it failsSelling insurance without saying so

Questions to ask about any yield (for study)

  1. Who is paying this, and why?
  2. What happens to the yield if prices fall or users leave?
  3. What risks am I taking that are not shown?
  4. Has it survived a market crash?
  5. Can the team change the rules or take the funds?
  6. If it is far above other rates, what is the catch?

Real yield after reward-token losses

Change the advertised yield, the share paid in reward tokens and how much those tokens fall to see the real yield. A teaching model.

Adjust Advertised yield (% a year), Share paid in reward tokens (%), Reward-token price fall (%) and see Real yield after the fall (% a year) change.

Check what you just learned

1. A very high yield with no explained source is usually:
  • Free money
  • Guaranteed
  • Paid by new deposits, reward-token printing or hidden risk (correct)
  • Insured

Ask who pays.

Check what you just learned

1. Yield paid from new users' deposits is:
  • Guaranteed
  • Sustainable
  • Insured
  • Unsustainable (correct)

A Ponzi structure.

Key terms: flip and sort

TWAP
Time-weighted average price
Peg
The intended price of a stablecoin
Reflexivity
A system whose price affects its own backing
Reward token
A token paid to users as an incentive
Circuit breaker
A rule that halts activity on odd data
Real yield
Return from genuine fees or interest
keyPoints: Sustainable yield comes from fees, borrower interest or network rewards.
Reward tokens and new deposits are fragile sources.

modules.title: DeFi risk, security and responsibility
modules.summary: The patterns behind exploits, how to review a protocol, and the legal and ethical care that builders and users owe.
modules.outcome: You can review a protocol's risks, explain the common exploit patterns and state what responsible building and honest communication require.
modules.intro: DeFi has lost billions to a small number of repeating mistakes. Knowing them is the best protection, whether you build, audit or merely use these systems. This module gathers the patterns, a due-diligence method and the responsibilities that come with handling other people's money.

topics.title: The patterns behind the losses
topics.html:
Common exploit patterns
PatternHow it worksDefence
Oracle manipulationAttacker moves a price source, then profits from a protocol that trusts itTime-weighted or multi-source prices, sanity checks
ReentrancyA callback re-enters before state is updatedChecks-effects-interactions and guards
Flash-loan governance attackBorrow voting power for one transaction to pass a proposalSnapshots of voting power taken before proposals, time delays
Rounding and share-price attacksFirst depositor or tiny amounts exploit integer divisionMinimum liquidity, virtual shares, rounding in the protocol's favour
Admin key compromiseA stolen key upgrades or drains contractsMulti-signature control, time-locks, key custody
Bridge failuresVerification flaws or few keys guard a huge poolStrong verification, limits and monitoring
Rug pullsCreators drain liquidity or mint endlesslyLocked liquidity, capped admin powers, transparency

Check what you just learned

1. Which defence best addresses flash-loan governance attacks?
  • Snapshotting voting power before a proposal so borrowed tokens cannot vote (correct)
  • Faster blocks
  • Lower fees
  • Public chat

Voting power must not be rentable for a moment.

Check what you just learned

1. A rug pull depends on:
  • Slow blocks
  • Unchecked admin or creator power (correct)
  • Low fees
  • Public code

Limit the powers.
keyPoints: A few patterns cause most losses: oracles, reentrancy, governance, rounding, keys, bridges and rug pulls.
Each has a known defence.

topics.title: Reviewing a protocol
topics.html:
A due-diligence checklist (for study)
AreaQuestions
Code and auditsWho audited it, when, with what findings? Was the audited code the deployed code?
Admin powersWho can upgrade or pause? Is it multi-signature and time-locked? Are parameters bounded?
DependenciesWhich oracles, bridges and tokens does it rely on? What if they fail?
EconomicsWhere does the yield come from? What happens in a crash?
Track recordHow long has it run with real value? How did it behave in stress?
TransparencyIs the team known? Is documentation honest about risks?
Monitoring and responseIs there a bug bounty, a security contact and an incident plan?
LimitsAre there caps that bound the damage of a failure?

How to read an audit report

  1. Read the scope: what was and was not reviewed.
  2. Look at the number and severity of findings.
  3. See whether serious findings were fixed and re-checked.
  4. Check that the deployed code matches the audited commit.
  5. Remember that an audit is a snapshot and not a guarantee.

Check what you just learned

1. Why check that deployed code matches the audited commit?
  • It is a tradition
  • Auditors insist
  • Changes after the audit are unreviewed and may contain bugs (correct)
  • It saves gas

Only the audited code was reviewed.

Check what you just learned

1. A protocol with unlimited upgrade power in one key is:
  • Insured
  • Safe
  • Audited
  • High risk (correct)

A single point of failure.
keyPoints: Review code and audits, admin powers, dependencies, economics, history and response plans.
An audit is a snapshot, not a guarantee.

topics.title: Building and speaking responsibly
topics.html:
Responsibilities of builders

  • Start on test networks and keep caps small at launch.
  • Limit and delay admin power, and publish it.
  • Get independent audits for anything holding value.
  • Never promise returns; explain risks plainly.
  • Publish a security contact and a bug bounty.
  • Have an incident plan and use it honestly.
  • Take legal advice: rules on exchanges, lending and tokens differ by country.
Honest and misleading communication
HonestMisleading
Past performance is not a guide to the futureGuaranteed 40% yearly returns
You can lose all of your depositRisk-free yield
Audited by X on this date; findings are listed hereFully audited and totally safe
The team can pause the contractCompletely decentralised, nobody controls anything (when an admin key exists)

DeFi is sometimes marketed as 'trustless'. In practice, users trust code, authors, oracles, admins and governance. Honest builders name those trust assumptions instead of hiding them.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is 'trustless' often misleading?
  • Users still trust code, authors, oracles and administrators (correct)
  • It is a technical term only
  • Contracts are never trusted
  • It means free

Name the real trust assumptions.

Watch out

Education only. Nothing in this course is financial, legal or investment advice, and DeFi can lose all of your money.

Check what you just learned

1. Promising guaranteed returns is:
  • Good practice
  • Misleading and often unlawful (correct)
  • Required
  • Normal

Never promise returns.

Key terms: flip and sort

Exploit
An attack that takes advantage of a flaw
Rug pull
A creator abandoning a project after taking funds
Due diligence
Careful investigation before relying on something
Audit
An independent security review
Bug bounty
A reward for reporting flaws responsibly
Trust assumption
A thing you must rely on being honest or correct
keyPoints: Builders owe users honesty, small launches, limited powers, audits and response plans.
Name the trust assumptions instead of claiming 'trustless'.
